---
title: "How to read the measurements"
subtitle: "Data source, chart construction, and limits"
---

## Data used here

The project uses the Driveline Baseball Research & Development
[OpenBiomechanics Project](https://github.com/drivelineresearch/openbiomechanics).
Its pitching release includes 411 trials. The full-signal charts use shoulder
rotation velocity and elbow moment sampled over time; the pitch comparison
uses the one-row-per-trial point-of-interest (POI) summary file.

## How the charts are built

- The shoulder-velocity and elbow-moment signals are joined by trial ID and
  timestamp. Only matched rows with both measurements present are plotted.
- For the time-course chart, each trial's timestamps are rescaled to its own
  recorded duration. The median and interquartile range are then summarized
  across trials at each relative-time percentage.
- The peak-moment distribution uses one maximum signed elbow-moment value per
  trial, so trials with more sampled timestamps do not contribute more often.
- The pitch comparison uses one row per trial with available pitch speed and
  peak elbow varus moment. Its trend line summarizes the observed association.

## Important limits

These are descriptive biomechanics data, not a clinical study. Repeated
timestamps from one trial are related observations, not separate pitches.
Relative time helps align signal shapes but does not identify a shared
biomechanical event. A joint moment is not a direct measurement of tissue
stress or injury, and the dataset does not provide confirmed injury outcomes.
The charts should not be used to diagnose an athlete or estimate individual
injury risk.

See the project's [pitching data dictionary](https://github.com/drivelineresearch/openbiomechanics/blob/main/baseball_pitching/data/data_dictionary.csv)
for field definitions and the [data license](https://github.com/drivelineresearch/openbiomechanics/blob/main/LICENSE-DATA.md)
for terms of use.
